The second sentence, which says nothing in the order shall be deemed to modify or diminish functions assigned by other orders, is a rule of construction attached to that revocation, creates no command and has no term of its own; disclosed alternative: a reviewer may treat it as a continuing non-derogation rule. research_rationale:
EO:11794 (signed 1974-07-11; 39 FR 25937, Federal Register of July 15, 1974) revokes Executive Order No. 10958 of August 14, 1961 on the Civil Defense medical and food stockpiles (first sentence, issued under Reorganization Plan No. 1 of 1958) and adds a second sentence providing that nothing in the order shall be deemed to modify or diminish the civil defense and emergency preparedness planning functions that Executive Order Nos. 11490 and 10952 and the orders listed in that sentence assign to the Secretary of Agriculture, the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare, the Secretary of Defense and the Administrator of General Services. Identity: the registered original is the Federal Register printing in jobs/fr-originals; number, date and subject agree with the census register (the signing date is OCR-garbled in the text and taken from the register and the filing line, "Filed 7-11-74"). Inventory: the dossier's one clause covers both sentences; the second sentence is a rule of construction that protects functions assigned by other orders and assigns nothing itself. The first sentence ("is hereby revoked.") is a one-time revocation performed on signing; it has no effective-date or delay wording, so I read it as taking effect on 1974-07-11. The second sentence has no term of its own; because it only says what the revocation shall not be taken to do, it has nothing to operate on once the revocation is performed, and it protects functions that continue, if at all, under their own orders (EO 11490 was itself revoked by Executive Order 12656, section 2901, signed November 18, 1988, which this record does not rely on as an end). A reviewer may read the second sentence as a continuing non-derogation rule; I treat it as part of the same spent clause because it creates no command, and I disclose the alternative. Searches, chosen after reading their coverage notes (all complete, none with a coverage warning): the U.S. Code search (release point 119-121, citations of the order by number in statute text and notes; edition current through 2026-10-09) recorded 0 hits; the eCFR point-in-time search as of 2026-10-14 with GovInfo CFR bulk XML recorded 0 hits; the Federal Register catalog disposition-note search (1937 onward) recorded 0 hits for this order. I also searched every held order text (the Cruden held-text search, 33118 readable files) for the order's number; the only held texts that cite it are its own Federal Register printing. I found no held order that revokes, amends or suspends it.
